content:
“MoMMAs Voices transforms pain into purpose by empowering mothers and families to use their lived experiences as catalysts for change in maternal healthcare.”

How did MoMMAs Voices start? Can you share your story with us?

MoMMAs Voices was established in 2018 by the Preeclampsia Foundation to amplify the voices of those who have experienced pregnancy and childbirth complications or loss, particularlyamong historically marginalized communities. The program began with seed funding from theMerck for Mothers program, and followed the passing of the Act to Save Moms, which helped to establish and support funding for maternal mortality review committees in all 50 US states. The initiative was also inspired by individuals like Program Director Nicole Purnell, who, after losing her son to preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome in 2005, became a dedicated advocate formaternal health. Her personal journey and others’ underscores the importance of integrating patient experiences into healthcare improvements.

What leads mothers and families to become involved in MoMMAs Voices,and how does sharing their experience help towards transformative progress in reproductive healthcare?

Mothers and families often come to MoMMAs Voices seeking purpose after experiencing trauma, loss, or complications during pregnancy, childbirth, or postpartum. They turn their pain into purpose—not just for their own healing, but to ensure that no other family has to face the same challenges alone or unheard. By becoming certified as a Patient Family Partner (PFP), individuals are empowered to use their lived experience as a catalyst for change. The PFP training equips them to work directly with healthcare providers, hospital systems, and researchers—bringing the patient voice to the table where decisions are made. Their insights, grounded in personal journeys, are essential to shaping care strategies that are not only clinically effective but also compassionate and human-centered.

This partnership helps bridge the gap between medical expertise and the realities families face.Whether it’s improving communication, preventing complications, or rethinking how support is offered after birth, these changes are made possible because someone was brave enough to speak up—not for themselves, but for the next mother, the next baby, the next family. It’s advocacy driven by empathy. It’s change led by those who’ve lived it. And it’s a reminder that when we share our stories, we don’t just honor what we’ve been through—we create a future where others don’t have to go through it the same way.

What was the most unexpected or transformative part of MoMMAs Voices journey?

A significant milestone for MoMMAs Voices was receiving funding from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to expand their engagement with state perinatal quality collaborators. This support has enabled the integration of patient voices into quality improvement projects, particularly focusing on substance use disorder and maternal mental health, thereby bridging the gap between patient experiences and healthcare practices.

Can you share an example with us about how the Lived Experience Integration for providers influences or shapes a change in practice or education in maternal/reproductive care?

MoMMAs Voices, in collaboration with the Alliance for Innovation on Maternal Health (AIM), launched the Lived Experience Integration into Quality Improvement Community of Learning (COL). What began as an eight-week educational series has evolved into a four-week program that has now trained healthcare teams across 45 states. By partnering with certified Patient Family Partners, providers gain critical insights from real patient experiences—leading to more respectful, equitable, and patient-centered care practices.

MoMMAs Voices was born in the U.S. healthcare context, which is largely privatized. From your perspective, how can the lived experience insights and advocacy approaches from this initiative inform policy change in countries with national health systems, like those in the EU?

While MoMMAs Voices operates within the U.S. healthcare system, its emphasis on integrating patient experiences into care can be universally applied. National health systems in the EU can adopt similar frameworks by establishing partnerships between patients and providers, ensuring that healthcare policies and practices are informed by those directly affected. This approach promotes patient-centered care and can lead to systemic improvements across diverse healthcare models.

Were there moments where you felt truly heard or, conversely, deeply unseen by the system?

Many participants in MoMMAs Voices have shared feelings of being overlooked or unheard during their healthcare experiences. By joining the program, they found a platform to voice their stories and contribute to meaningful change, transforming feelings of isolation into empowerment and advocacy. “Aha” moments both big and small happen anytime that a patient family partner watches their lived experience enlighten the way that healthcare providers manage patient care.


 Does MoMMAs Voices believe it is important for healthcare systems to actively integrate lived experiences (particularly from those who have gone through pregnancy loss, birth trauma, or complex reproductive journeys) into policy, training, and service design?

Absolutely! MoMMAs Voices advocates for the integration of lived experiences into all facets of healthcare, including policy development, provider training, and service design. By doing so, healthcare systems can ensure that care is empathetic, responsive, and tailored to the real needs of patients.

As a survivor-led initiative, where would you most like to see progress made in reproductive and maternal healthcare—whether in patient communication, research priorities, emotional support, or systemic reform?

MoMMAs Voices emphasizes the need for systemic reform that prioritizes patient voices. This includes enhancing patient-provider communication, directing research towards patient-identified priorities, offering robust emotional support services, and addressing disparities in care to ensure equity across all populations.

Looking ahead, what is your vision?

MoMMAs Voices envisions a healthcare system where patient experiences are central to care delivery. By continuing to train Patient Family Partners, collaborating with healthcare providers, and influencing policy, the program aims to create a future where every mother receives respectful, equitable, and effective care throughout her reproductive journey.

content:
“Understanding all facets of infertility is the first step to new non-intrusive treatments. I imagine a future where every infertility case will be cured therapeutically”

Elina Aleksejeva-Zagura, PhD

„All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way“ Leo Tolstoy

Understanding all facets of infertility is the first step to new non-intrusive treatments. I imagine a future where every infertility case will be cured therapeutically.

Studying the underlying causes of infertility made me realize that there is a huge heterogeneity among patients seeking help of assisted reproductive technologies (ART) to conceive. Describing the field, I would rephrase the famous quote by Leo Tolstoy: „All fertile families are alike; each infertile family is infertile in its own way.“ Among known pathologies, numbers of which distribute equally among men and women, many infertility cases are unexplained. Sadly, approximately 30% of couples who undergo infertility treatments, sometimes spanning years, are left without a child (1). This highlights the unmet clinical need in reproductive medicine. It also complicates the execution of clinical trials for new innovations –  imagine the challenge to form proper study and control groups when there are so many variables and, unfortunately, the grey area of unknowns! The high failure-rate in innovation is in fact due to uncertainties associated with uncharted technologies and knowledge gaps in the disease etiology.

Reducing the invasiveness, increasing the safety and efficiency

The birth of the first in vitro conceived baby in 1978 heralded a new era in reproduction that is extremely invasive. Taking the oocytes out of the body, injecting sperm into oocyte, taking biopsy from an early embryo – individuals born by applying some of these techniques are currently not older than 33 years. So far no debilitating effects on health due to ART have been observed, although it is associated with modestly higher risks for premature birth and lower birth-weight. Besides increasing safety, there are other benefits to reducing the invasiveness of these techniques.

Tissue biopsy is characteristic only to the site from which it is taken and therefore cannot circumvent diagnostic errors due to tissue mosaicism if it occurs, however non-invasive biomarkers would likely represent the tissue as a whole. My main focus has been the development of non-invasive test to detect the window of embryo implantation of endometrium, hoping it could increase accuracy of endometrial receptivity assessment and decrease the treatment duration. We have gathered enough evidence to prove that uterine fluid components called extracellular vesicles can be used to monitor the state of endometrium (2,3), however it cannot be implemented in the clinic yet. Why not? Because what is needed is a fast test that could facilitate a snap-decision about endometrial readiness and embryo transfer in the same cycle.

We have the biomarkers and now a technology must be developed that would meet the time-requirement. It should be a point-of-care test to fulfil its full clinical potential. Since biomarker discovery study equipped us with a lot of data, we also found some candidate molecules which have therapeutic potential, which could reach (pre)-clinical validation one day. There’s still a long way to go!

At the intersection of science and business

During the years I spent at CELVIA I not only learned, I actually lived through lessons that I did not have in the educational programme during my studies at university. There are many blind spots in infertility etiology that must be filled with basic research, however innovating healthcare requires that the curiosity and open-mindedness of a scientist is applied with the ability to recognize features necessary for commercial viability. It is essential to define the minimal requirements for the success of the product or service before development, so you know objectively which features of technology must be achieved at each developmental stage. The importance of patenting cannot be neglected. I think it is especially clever to patent and then do research that broadens the applicability of the patent – although I myself have not been as clever yet! Finally, engaging with stakeholders, doctors and patients, can be useful as it helps to discover and fine-tune the actual clinical need and questions to be asked.

Sculpting (in)fertility awareness through ceramics

Working on a topic that is so intimately tied with existential choices, I have felt the responsibility to share my knowledge and raise (in)fertility awareness. I think people should be equipped with accurate knowledge to make informed choices in family planning, not to be swayed by marketing or myths. I was lucky enough to discover themes such as ovarian aging, egg freezing and miscarriages in the works of a contemporary artist Kris Lemsalu. This opened up a possibility to reach new people and thereby increase inclusivity in scientific communication. Coincidentally, art enriches life and ART gives opportunity to new life.

Kris Lemsalu

Whole alone 2

(2015)

title: Innovator Voices: Rick Essers
excerpt: Challenges in business are a given, but it’s our response to them that defines our trajectory. Looking beyond the immediate obstacle, there lies a realm of opportunity and learning.
content:
Looking to the future, I envision universal access to reproductive care, and I am looking forward to a non-invasive, accurate, all-in-one methodology.

Rick Essers, PhD

Improving Reproductive Genetic Care: A Vision for the Future

My work centers on improving reproductive genetic care—a field that holds immense promise but also carries significant responsibility. Striking to me, is the broad scope of reproductive genetics namely empowering couples in their reproductive decision-making, addressing infertility, preventing genetic diseases, and ensuring healthier pregnancies. With such a broad scope, we should carefully navigate the development of novel techniques, always being mindful of ethical considerations and the need to ensure equitable access to these advancements on a global scale.

Looking to the future, I envision universal access to reproductive care, and I am looking forward to a non-invasive, accurate, all-in-one methodology. A key part of this vision includes developing a complete genomic atlas of early embryonic development, which would unravel the complex chromosomal dynamics of this stage. This would not only help improve the success rates of assisted reproductive technologies (ART) but also enhance our understanding of the intricate processes that shape early life.

A Field of Contrasts: Archaicism and Modernism

What surprised me about reproductive genetics is that it is a fascinating blend of archaicism and modernism. Some methodologies in use today feel outdated and understudied—for example, the exact mechanisms and effect of ovarian stimulation protocols, the controversies surrounding preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy (PGT-A), and the modest overall efficiency of PGT (~30%). Even the question of how well the trophectoderm (TE) biopsy truly represents the embryo remains unresolved. Yet, at the same time, the field is rapidly evolving, driven by technological advancements that have revolutionized both diagnostics and treatment approaches. We can now map the genome into more detail and can detect more types of aberrations than ever before. This dynamic tension makes the field both challenging and exhilarating to work in.

A personal area of interest within this space is the self-correction mechanisms of early life. These natural processes, where embryos can sometimes repair chromosomal abnormalities, remain a largely unexplored frontier. Models that propose depletion by apoptosis or limited propagation of aneuploid cells, trisomy/monosomy rescue, and preferential allocation of aneuploid cells to the placenta lineage. However, our current insights are humble, and this uncertainty makes it thrilling to pioneer research in this domain.

Moments of Impact: Connecting Research to Real Lives

One moment that profoundly shaped my perspective was my work on first-trimester pregnancy loss (Add DOI?: Prevalence of chromosomal alterations in first-trimester spontaneous pregnancy loss, Nature Medicine, 2023). This study had two key findings: First, using newer genomic techniques, we found that the proportion of pregnancy losses explained by genetic aberrations increased from ~50% to 67.8%. Second, we uncovered a tissue-specific nature of chromosomal aberrations, with a higher degrees of mosaic chromosomal imbalances observed in the embryonic lineage compared to the placental lineage in non-viable pregnancies.

What struck me most was how these findings were received. While the second message was far more difficult to uncover, it was the first—showing that genetic factors explain more losses than previously thought—that resonated most deeply with the public. For couples grieving a pregnancy loss, this was critical validation that they were not at fault. This experience underscored the importance of keeping the end users of our research—couples hoping for a child—at the forefront of our work.

Similarly, my retrospective study into a novel form of PGT (Preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy origin (PGT-AO) to enhance embryo selection: an integrative genomic and clinical study, submitted) revealed the direct impact of new methodologies on couples. The findings made it clear how much time, emotional distress, and loss could be prevented with more precise techniques. Moments like these remind me of the real-world significance of our research and the lives it can touch.

Collaboration and Connection: The Heart of Progress

These impactful studies were only possible through collaboration—between research groups, clinicians, laboratory personnel, analysts, and, most importantly, the couples themselves. Reproductive genetics is inherently a team effort, requiring interdisciplinary expertise and a shared commitment to advancing care.

On a personal note, as I’ve entered my thirties, stories of fertility challenges have become more common among my peers. Hearing these experiences has given me a renewed, deeply personal motivation to continue my research and contribute to solutions that can bring hope and healing to so many.

A Vision for Transformative Change

Looking ahead, I hope future generations will view my contributions as a meaningful step toward improving reproductive outcomes and advancing patient-centered care. If I could make one transformative change in reproductive medicine over the next decade, it would be to integrate a non-invasive, comprehensive genomic testing method into routine care. Such a tool would combine accuracy and efficiency while remaining accessible to all, eliminating many of the current barriers couples face.

Ultimately, I dream of a world where every couple has the opportunity to build the family they envision, supported by science that is compassionate, equitable, and precise. Reproductive genomic medicine has the power to transform lives, and I am honored to play a part in shaping its future.
